keep: Specify the outcome, not the method — and remember that reproducibility, not brilliance, is what the prize is for.
title: Finding Longitude
sub: The problem that ate a century
claim: A prize specified an outcome, not a method. It took sixty years, and no one was ever paid it in full.
lede: Latitude you can read off the sky. Longitude requires knowing what time it is somewhere else — which, at sea, in 1714, was a scientific impossibility with a national body count.
copy: Britain's Longitude Act of 1714 offered up to £20,000 for a practical method of determining longitude at sea, after a series of disasters made the problem politically unignorable. Two approaches competed. Lunar distances required good tables, clear skies, and about four hours of a navigator's arithmetic per fix. A sea-going clock accurate enough to carry Greenwich time across an ocean was considered impossible by every serious authority, because pendulums don't work on a moving ship and metal expands with heat.

John Harrison spent forty years being wrong in increasingly productive ways — H1, H2, H3, and finally H4, a large watch rather than a clock. On the 1761–62 crossing to Jamaica, Harrison put it at 5.1 seconds slow after eighty-one days, but only after an allowance for the watch's rate that he declared once the ship had arrived, and the Board called the trial inconclusive. On the second voyage, to Barbados in 1764, it lost 39.2 seconds in 47 days, inside the Act's narrowest limit. What happened next is where the popular story and the archives part company.

The popular version is a stitch-up by a jealous Astronomer Royal. The archival version, reconstructed from the Board of Longitude papers, is duller and more interesting: the Board was a committee applying a statutory test to a one-off handmade object that could not yet be reproduced by anyone else. Reproducibility was precisely the point of the statute — a method only one man in England can execute is not a method. Harrison was funded by the Board for decades. In 1765 a special Act paid him half the prize, £10,000, once he had explained the watch; the other half waited on proof that other makers could build it, and never came. Parliament gave him £8,750 more in 1773, as a grant rather than the prize. No one was ever paid the prize in full.

The prize model is the part worth stealing, and the part worth being careful about. It specified an outcome rather than a method, paid on demonstrated performance, and stayed open for decades — all things a grant committee cannot do. It also took sixty years and consumed one man's working life, and the winning technology arrived alongside a rival method the tables had finally made practical. Both halves are the lesson.

timeline.t: Four ships and around 1,400 men are lost off the Scilly Isles, partly through navigational error.
The Longitude Act offers up to £20,000 and creates the Board of Longitude.
The Commissioners of Longitude meet for the first time, on 30 June, and vote Harrison £500 for a better clock.
H4 crosses to Jamaica: 5.1 seconds slow after 81 days on Harrison's figure, after a rate allowance declared once the ship had landed. The Board calls the trial inconclusive.
On the voyage to Barbados H4 loses 39.2 seconds in 47 days; in February 1765 the Board agrees it kept time within the Act's narrowest limit.
A special Act pays Harrison half the prize, £10,000, once he has explained the mechanism so others can copy it.
Parliament grants a further £8,750, as a gift rather than the prize. The second half is never paid, to Harrison or to anyone.

figures.d: A carpenter turned clockmaker who solved a problem the Royal Society thought belonged to astronomy.
Astronomer Royal, villain of the popular account, and the man whose Nautical Almanac made lunars usable.
Made K1, the copy of H4 that proved the design was reproducible — the test that actually mattered.

facts.s: Harrison's Jamaica figure after 81 days, after a rate allowance of 2.66 seconds a day declared once the voyage was over: Jonathan R. Siegel, 'Law and Longitude', Tulane Law Review 84 (2009), pp. 18–19 and n. 93

H4's loss over 47 days on the 1764 Barbados voyage: National Maritime Museum, 'John Harrison and the Longitude problem' (2002), read in a mirror copy at pro.unibz.it after the original nmm.ac.uk address went dead
The half of the prize paid under the special Act of 1765, the £2,500 already advanced counted in: Siegel, 'Law and Longitude' (2009), pp. 24 and 32–33
Parliament's 1773 grant, £1,250 short of the outstanding half: Siegel, 'Law and Longitude' (2009), p. 26

contested: Dava Sobel's bestselling 'lone genius versus the establishment' framing has been substantially revised by historians working from the Board of Longitude archives. Harrison was funded by the Board for decades and was paid half the prize; the astronomers' objections were partly technical — a handmade one-off is not yet a method — rather than purely political.
changed: I read Sobel first, like everyone, and carried the villain version around for years. The archives changed my mind about Maskelyne specifically, and more usefully about the general shape: when an institution frustrates an inventor, the boring possibility is that the institution is enforcing a criterion the inventor hasn't met yet.
